analysis: Gilgit and Kohistani maá~ have late long-root accent compatible with the old oxytone, while Guresi máa~ is early. Buddruss also gives early Gilgit máa~, conflicting with Schmidt and Degener within the same named dialect. Mother is an irregular kinship noun with possessive and address forms, so cell alignment must precede an explanation, but the source conflict remains real until those cells are demonstrated to differ.
unresolved: Read the complete mother entries and possessive paradigms; do not force Buddruss into agreement by majority vote.

analysis: Palula móoṇ ‘nest’ has early accent and raised oo, compatible with inherited early long ā. The semantic change from dwelling to an animal's dwelling is straightforward; the older spider-web sense also refers to a constructed habitation. The retroflex nasal still requires its regular segmental context to be documented, but accent and vowel quality jointly support the inherited-root analysis.
unresolved: Inspect inflection and distinguish this family from other māna homonyms and Iranian house terms.

analysis: Palula móoṇuṣ, Biori máaṣ and Strand plural mʹôṣa preserve early prominence and reflect the old long-root formation. Gilgit mušáa instead accents a final long vowel and has lost much of the old stem; it must be analyzed separately from manúẓo under short-root mánuṣa. The old quantity distinction and modern inflectional formation supply independent reasons not to merge all human-word records.
unresolved: Identify the grammatical cell and derivation of mušáa and the source-specific Palula singular/plural relation.

analysis: Palula mhaaríi is a causative kill verb with an accented newer ending, while Gilgit mar- is a bare short-root citation. The causative's old long ā and Palula secondary aspiration distinguish it from die máara, but neither the different modern citation endings nor their accents can be compared as equivalent cells. Root quantity itself has diverged across languages and needs paradigm evidence.
unresolved: Align imperative, present and perfective kill forms and test whether Gilgit short a alternates under inflection.

analysis: Gilgit máaz and Kohistani/Guresi/Astori móos have early accent on inherited long ā. This contrasts directly with late moós ‘flesh’ from māṁsá in several of the same dialects. The month/flesh pair isolates inherited accent more closely than comparisons drawn from unrelated modern vowel qualities, although the old nasal and resulting segmental histories must still be retained in the table.
unresolved: Add independent Gilgit dictionary tokens and noun paradigms; preserve the distinct early máaz vowel quality rather than normalizing it to moos.

analysis: Strand mʹitr ‘blood brother’ is short and therefore lacks an early/late long-vowel opposition even though root prominence is explicit. The personal name mitraʹi adds final material and has its own naming/derivational accent; it should not count as a second direct sound reflex of the common noun. The blood-brother meaning provides reasonable semantic continuity with friend.
unresolved: Check whether the common noun is inherited or a learned/contact term and recover its inflected accent.

analysis: Palula míla ‘argue, quarrel’ is initially accented in the imperative citation, while miliǰʹi ‘mixed’ has additional resultative material carrying later prominence. The meeting/mixing/fighting senses support a common root, but the old finite final-root accent cannot be projected directly onto the imperative and resultative as if they were unchanged words.
unresolved: Establish the verb's conjugational accent pattern and the resultative suffix's productivity.

analysis: All four Schmidt Shina dialects give short mukh/muk ‘face’, so no two-mora contour is available. The presence versus absence of aspiration is dialectal segmental evidence, not evidence for distinct accent types. Independent dictionary face records are linked instead to múkhya, creating a duplicate/competing etymological assignment that must be reconciled before counting families.
unresolved: Choose between the simple noun and adjective using segmental and semantic evidence, and inspect inflected face forms for fixed versus mobile accent.

analysis: Short Palula/Gilgit/Kundal mukh ‘face’ overlaps the múkha family and supplies no long-vowel contour. Gilgit makhóoro ‘elder, chief’ has extra accented stem material and closely matches the chief sense of múkhya, making it a separate derivational problem. Sauji mukhá and Kalkoti mukhä ‘front’ retain a final vowel, but their source notation and grammatical functions differ from the bare face noun.
unresolved: Read leader morphology and distinguish ordinary face, relational front and chief formations; deduplicate the shared face lexeme.

analysis: Gilgit muč- ‘be released, escape’ matches the old passive valency, while Palula mučóo ‘open, untie’ is transitive and carries a modern conjugational ending. The old entry itself attests both accent positions, so there is no single inherited finite accent to test. The Palula transitive formation must also be distinguished from the old active muñcáti family.
unresolved: Compare full active/passive paradigms and determine whether the Palula citation is a later causative or transitive reassignment.

analysis: Gilgit moǰ- ‘save’ is a bare stem with no marked accent, and older infinitives accent newer endings. Its voiced palatal consonant distinguishes it from muč- ‘escape’, independently supporting an active/passive formation split within the same old root family. Modern citation differences therefore should not be reduced to one supposedly irregular accent correspondence.
unresolved: Recover finite accents and identify the source of the o/u alternation across cells and dialects.

analysis: Palula mung is short and cannot realize an early/late long-vowel contrast; Strand explicitly marks its single root vowel. Kundal muŋphil ‘groundnut’ is a compound or borrowed compound and supplies a different lexical history. Gilgit bukák ‘beans’ has neither the expected root segments nor a transparently documented derivation from mudga, so its inherited-family link needs independent support rather than an accent exception label.
unresolved: Investigate bukák as a replacement or separately derived pulse name and exclude it from direct mudga sound-law tests pending evidence.

analysis: Palula múṣṭi ‘fist’ and múṭi ‘forearm’ retract accent to the first short syllable despite the old final í; both modern nuclei remain, making this a true accent-position question. Gilgit muṭ is monosyllabic, while Guresi/Astori miṭhíj/miṭhíjo ‘shoulder’ have later derivational material and final-root accent. Retained ṣṭ in one Palula lexeme versus simplified ṭ in another suggests lexical or borrowing stratification as well as semantic differentiation.
unresolved: Read inflections and borrowing evidence for the two Palula forms; analyze the shoulder suffix separately and retain the retraction residual.

analysis: Gilgit múzal ‘pestle’ retains first-syllable accent after final a is lost, leaving two short syllables. This gives useful evidence for accent-locus retention outside long monosyllables and without attraction to a later long vowel. Turner's alternative *muṣala/*muśala and non-Indo-Aryan origin discussion concern segmental variants; the actual modern z supports analysis of a specific inherited stratum rather than all variants at once.
unresolved: Inspect the oblique paradigm and compare Palula muuṣoó ‘elbow’, a different nominal formation and meaning.

analysis: Palula múutr preserves early accent on inherited long ū with tr retained. Kundal mutrā̂̃ and Sauji mutre add vocalic material whose grammatical or derivational status must be established before comparing accent position. The Palula form is a clean retention example, while the other languages provide segmental cognacy without a straightforward shared citation cell.
unresolved: Determine Kundal's final nasal vowel notation and the case/number of Sauji mutre.

analysis: Gilgit múuṭo and Kohistani múutho modify ‘milk’ in the curds expressions. They have early long-root accent before an unaccented adjective ending despite the old oxytone participle. This fits the root-final extended adjective pattern; the space before dut is a syntactic boundary, not a second accent within one lexical word. Old ū remains long, and the old rt cluster has different modern consonantal outcomes.
unresolved: Recover the adjective's independent inflection and separate its token from the following milk noun in quantitative parsing.

input: mū́la, mūlaka ‘radish’, mūlikā ‘root used in magic’
analysis: Gilgit mulíi/mulií ‘root’ has final accented ī and a shortened initial vowel, whereas Palula mulái ‘radish’ has an added final formation. The old entry independently supplies radish and feminine derivatives, making those preferable morphological comparisons to a single unextended mūla headword. Schmidt's late mulií and Degener's early mulíi nevertheless conflict within the same modern formation and must be retained as a source difference.
unresolved: Verify both Gilgit source readings and paradigms; establish the radish ending without assigning unattested old derivative accents.

analysis: Palula mring ‘markhor’ and Gilgit briŋ ‘bird’ have short nuclei and no two-mora contour contrast. Initial m-to-b strengthening in Shina and the nasalized final development provide segmental evidence for the family despite semantic divergence between kinds of animals. The short modern outcome must not be counted as late solely from the old final accent.
unresolved: Recover inflected accents and assess the specific semantic histories independently of the quantity classification.

analysis: Gilgit múu~o ‘dead’ is an early-accented participial adjective with a final ending, while Palula máara is the present/imperative citation of ‘die’, not a direct segmental reflex of mr̥tá. The latter enters this family through lexical/paradigmatic linking and must be replaced by actual muṛ- perfective cells for sound-change analysis. Chilas lik/lič ‘died’ may be a suppletive replacement and requires separate justification.
unresolved: Recover actual Palula past forms, exclude citation-form leakage, and explain the newly long Gilgit participial vowel.

analysis: Palula méeṭi has early long-root accent and final unaccented i, compatible with the independently initial-accented old feminine. Root length and fronting require the cluster/umlaut chronology, since old syllabic r was not a long ē. This offers a useful contrast to final-accented fly machíi, whose old -ikā formation was also initially accented but later followed a different feminine pattern.
unresolved: Establish the intermediate vowel quality and exact declension, and test why some feminine formations retain root accent while others shift.

analysis: All four Schmidt Shina dialects míṣṭo/míṣṭho/míṣṭhu accent the short final root syllable before an unaccented gender vowel. The outcome accords with the extended adjective class despite old final-a accent. Kundal miṣṭ has lost the ending and lacks a comparable long-vowel contour. Sauji mušṓ ‘sweet’ is finally accented and differently reduced, so its exact formation cannot be assumed identical to Shina ‘good’.
unresolved: Read Sauji adjective inflection and distinguish its final o from Shina's unaccented gender ending.

analysis: Strand mʹinḍ ‘ram’ has no plausible direct segmental or semantic derivation from mḗkhalā ‘girdle’. Turner 10310, whose digits transpose the last two digits of 10301, is mēṇḍha ‘ram’ and independently lists miṇḍha variants. This is strong evidence for a reference-number error, not an accentual sound change. The corrected old family has no marked accent, so correction removes a false accented-input datum.
unresolved: Verify the source website or original import reference to locate where the transposition arose; retain the research correction separately from the DB.

analysis: Palula míi and Gilgit/Astori míi~ have early prominence compatible with old ē accent and subsequent contraction/raising. Guresi mií~ is late in the same comparative source, while Kohistani myú~ and Degener míu have more complex vowel sequences. This is a genuine dialectal contour residual until differences in grease versus marrow formation or inflection are demonstrated.
unresolved: Verify the Guresi table against original print and analyze unequal-vowel sequences and semantic/case distinctions.

analysis: Gilgit miriǰ- belongs to a fuller derived die stem, while other citations represent infinitival or future cells. It must be compared jointly with mar- 9871 and the mr̥tá perfective 10278 as one historical paradigm with different stem formations. A bare stem without accent supplies no independent outcome, and older future marks belong to their actual endings.
unresolved: Reconstruct the present/passive stem distribution from full paradigms and avoid treating the three database families as independent verbs.

analysis: Shina yúum/yúu~ has early long-root prominence after severe contraction of an irregular old stem. Palula ǰhangaár is segmentally much more complex and may reflect another formation or contact word, not a direct unchanged nominative yákr̥t. The old genitive yaknás independently demonstrates accent and stem alternation; therefore the nominative headword alone cannot predict every modern liver word.
unresolved: Investigate the Palula liver word's internal/contact etymology and compare Kalkoti low-toned ǰä̀gär; identify which old stem underlies Shina.

analysis: Gilgit ya~c̣h is a short nasalized monosyllable, so it supplies no early/late long-vowel contrast. Derived yac̣halítu ‘mad’ and yac̣halyār ‘madness’ contain additional material and independent accents. The linked holo/olo forms lack the root's obvious segments and should be treated as possible lexical equivalents or replacements until a source explains their relation.
unresolved: Check the original comparative entry for synonym-link leakage and recover the demon noun's paradigm.

analysis: Ashret yáandr is early-accented but Biori yandr is short; Gilgit yó~r and Guresi yo~ṣ also do not show a clear long-vowel mora contrast in these transcriptions. Thus an old oxytone can lose its final accent onto a short root, followed by later Ashret lengthening with early alignment. It need not behave like preserved-long-root kālá > kaál. The retained ndr cluster in Palula also argues against treating its aa as simple compensation for total cluster loss.
unresolved: Read noun mobility and verify the timing of Ashret lengthening relative to apocope and accent docking.

analysis: Palula yúu has early long-vowel accent after contraction involving v and final a. The old first vowel was short but initially accented, so this differs both from old-long-root retention and from later lengthening of a closed a monosyllable. Older Sauji and Shina yū/yō support cognacy and vowel development but lack comparable contour marking.
unresolved: Reconstruct the glide-vowel sequence and compare the parallel numeral náva > núu without assuming identical intermediate quantity.

analysis: Shina yap/yab and Biori yab are short monosyllables; Ashret yáab is early-long. The Biori comparison supports later Ashret lengthening after loss of the old finally accented feminine material, explaining why an old oxytone does not yield a late vowel here. The old vy sequence and b reflex require a segmental intermediary, but a preserved old long first vowel is not available.
unresolved: Inspect inflected forms and test the wider short-monosyllable lengthening rule against this unaspirated control.

analysis: Palula yhíi/Biori yíi accents the citation ending after substantial contraction or stem reduction, whereas Gilgit yayoók is an infinitive and Kundal yɛ an imperative. Their cell differences and come/go semantic organization prevent a direct comparison of old yā́ti with every modern whole word. Kalkoti yuun has a low-tone counterpart in Hultman's analysis associated with lost aspiration, but HKAT itself marks no tone.
unresolved: Align motion-verb cells, identify the aspiration's historical layer and link source-specific Kalkoti forms.

analysis: Palula ǰhií~ and Gilgit ǰuú/ǰuú~ have late accent despite the old initial long-root accent. Both show extensive consonant loss and a surviving long vowel, making this a strong counterexample to unconditional retention of old barytonesis. Feminine long-ā morphology and contraction or later inflectional reaccentuation are plausible conditioning factors, but must be established independently; the old masculine variant is also initially accented.
unresolved: Inspect louse paradigms and compare other old feminine ā-stems before selecting contraction or analogical reaccentuation.

analysis: Gilgit rac̣h- ‘guard’ gives a short bound stem without accent marking; the older infinitives add their own accented endings. The cluster correspondence is useful for inheritance but does not turn an unaccented stem citation into a measured contour. The old finite accent must be compared with equivalent finite or imperative cells.
unresolved: Recover the guard verb's paradigm from the primary glossary material.

analysis: Palula ráaǰ and Biori short rhaǰ support early prominence with later Ashret lengthening, rather than preservation of an old long vowel. Gilgit raǰóṭi ‘string’ and raǰóoṭo ‘larger rope’ have size/gender derivational material that carries the accent; their second-syllable prominence is not a direct sound change of rájju's first accent. The short versus long o within those derivatives needs its own morphological explanation.
unresolved: Read the two Gilgit paradigms and verify the aspiration discrepancy between Palula dialects.

analysis: Gilgit ran- is a short unaccented bound stem, with older infinitives and passives displaying their own suffixes. The old causative formation and nasal cluster help explain the stem but provide no directly observed modern root accent. Kohistani cook versus Guresi be cooked must remain distinct valency cells.
unresolved: Recover active, passive and perfective paradigms and determine whether short a/u alternation is cell-conditioned.

analysis: Gilgit ra-/ray- ‘say’ is linked here, while the same infinitival word is linked elsewhere to rásati. Loss of p versus a s-to-y development are competing segmental histories that modern accent cannot decide by itself. Bound stems are unaccented in the citation and the infinitive's final accent belongs to a newer formation.
unresolved: Evaluate the competing speech etymologies through dialectal consonant correspondences and deduplicate shared modern entries.

analysis: Gilgit raš ‘eyesight, vision’ is short after loss of m and final i. Its meaning remains within the old ray/light semantic field. Because the modern nucleus is short, the old oxytone cannot be scored as an observed late contour; this is another negative control against obligatory lengthening after cluster reduction.
unresolved: Recover case forms for accent mobility and specify the śm cluster's regular segmental outcome.

analysis: Gilgit rayoók accents the modern infinitival ending; Kohistani razōnu and Guresi ražōnu preserve consonants potentially relevant to choosing between rásati and rápati. The root etymology must be evaluated from those correspondences and semantics, not by matching the old initial accent to a suffix-accented infinitive. Shared speech entries count only once in lexical statistics.
unresolved: Inspect the comparative argument for s/z/ž/y and distinguish it from p loss in the alternative analysis.

analysis: Gilgit ráa ‘king’ retains early prominence on the old long root, while raǰoó ‘royal’ accents final derived material and preserves j. The old entry independently provides suffix-accented rājaká, so the royal derivative has a plausible separate input rather than being an exception to king's accent retention. The retained j also warns that the derivative may reflect a different chronological or borrowing layer.
unresolved: Check the royal formation's morphology and contact history before claiming direct inheritance from rājaká.

analysis: All four Shina dialects ráati retain early root accent and a final i, while Palula raát ‘night plus day as a measure’ is late and lacks that vowel. Final-vowel loss in a feminine or measure-word formation is an independently visible difference that may condition reaccentuation; the old long barytone alone does not predict Palula. Older Palula rōt further suggests a raised-vowel or source layer needing reconciliation. Kalkoti ràat has lexical low tone unexplained by a corresponding Palula aspirate.
unresolved: Compare ordinary night versus duration/counting constructions and their paradigms, and verify older rōt and the Kalkoti low-tone source.

analysis: Strand rʹûpo ‘silver’ has early root accent with a final nominal vowel, compatible with the old initial long-root adjective/substance formation. Gilgit rupáai ‘rupee’ is a currency term with a distinct modern formation and likely contact history; its later accent should not be treated as a direct exception to silver. Older short silver citations supply no mora contrast.
unresolved: Document the currency donor and distinguish inherited silver from borrowed money terminology.

analysis: Palula loomúṭ ‘deodar’ is also recorded by CDIAL explicitly as lō-múṭ under *lōka 11120, alongside lōu ‘resin, tar’. The accent falls on the independently recognizable tree constituent muṭ, so it is not an unexplained shift within a reflex of rṓka alone. The two DB links represent alternative analyses of the first constituent and duplicate the same modern compound; the old rōka family itself also allows both accent positions.
unresolved: Verify the semantic connection of resin/light and deodar in the original entry, and keep first-constituent etymology separate from compound accent.

input: rṓha; compare the broader ruh verbal paradigm
analysis: Gilgit ruú~ ‘heal’ is late-accented, but its verbal gloss and accompanying wa- indicate that the old noun rṓha may enter a modern predicate or light-verb construction. Deriving a bare verb directly from the noun's citation accent would therefore be unsafe. Loss of h and contraction are additional plausible sources of altered mora alignment that require an explicit intermediate.
unresolved: Read the full Degener entry to determine grammatical structure and whether ruu is a nominal predicate or verb stem.

analysis: Strand rohʹiṇ ‘urial’ accents the short second vowel, whereas the older rōhiṇá ‘male wild sheep’ retains an additional accented ending. The input is an old feminine cow term and the modern referent is a male wild sheep, so both gender formation and semantic reanalysis intervene. Initial old prominence is not retained transparently, and source/cell differences cannot be dismissed as mere notation.
unresolved: Check the animal's masculine/feminine paradigm and the old rōhi- formation before proposing reaccentuation or borrowing.

input: laghú and independently linked extended formations
analysis: Palula lhoóku and Gilgit loóko have late long-root accent before an unaccented gender vowel, while older lohóko preserves a less contracted stage. This parallels madhurá > mhoóru: root-final accent is compatible with the adjective class, but mora alignment differs from early tíiṇu. Loss/reorganization of medial aspiration and contraction provide independently visible conditions for a late subclass.
unresolved: Recover the exact old extension, inspect adjective paradigms, and test the proposed VhV-contraction subclass rather than grouping by modern tone alone.

analysis: Palula láanga is early-accented in the imperative citation, while Gilgit laŋ- is unmarked and laŋiǰ- ‘die’ includes further intransitive morphology. The old entry contains multiple finite formations, so the broad causative headword does not uniquely supply every modern verb's accent. The semantic development ‘cross over’ to ‘die’ may be lexicalized within a derived stem.
unresolved: Compare corresponding imperative and finite cells and identify the derivational accent of -iǰ-.

analysis: Palula laǰíǰa ‘be ashamed’ accents the i of an expanded intransitive stem. The old jj and middle-voice meaning support the root relationship, but the modern iǰ formation is additional material, not a preserved second vowel of lajjátē. Its accent should be tested against the productive modern conjugational class.
unresolved: Recover the shame verb's paradigm and compare other -iǰa intransitives independently of etymological accent.

analysis: Palula lháaya/Biori lháaye have early root prominence after bh weakening and aspiration relocation. Gilgit lai-/lay- is a bare stem, and Kohistani lhaunu an infinitive; these cannot be counted as equivalent accent-bearing cells. The unequal vowel/glide sequence also requires source-based parsing before inferring a long nucleus and mora alignment.
unresolved: Read finite and imperative paradigms and establish the sequence of contraction and root-vowel lengthening.

analysis: Gilgit niláawo has early prominence on its second long root vowel before a final ending. Its initial n and consonant order favor the independently attested niṭāla variant over direct derivation from lalā́ṭa. Because that variant is not independently accented in the entry, transferring lalā́ṭa's medial accent would overstate the evidence even though the modern position happens to agree.
unresolved: Establish the variant's source accent if available and document the ṭ/l/w history and noun extension.

analysis: Palula lhoóṇ and Kohistani/Guresi luúṇi have late long-root prominence after contraction of the old multivocalic stem. Shina's final i is additional or retained feminine material, so the shared late root contour cannot be reduced to identical surface apocope. Kundal nū̃ has a distinct initial-consonant development and uninformative legacy tone notation. Kalkoti lùun offers a separate low-tone comparison associated with aspiration loss.
unresolved: Determine the final i formation and test competing old intermediates without importing accents into unaccented reconstructions.

analysis: Gilgit leéc̣ is late-accented while Kohistani léec̣i is early with a surviving final vowel. This resembles other pairs where the dialect losing final vocalic material has later mora alignment, but the old stem also undergoes contraction and tr affrication. The independently visible i difference supplies a testable conditioning feature rather than an outcome-defined class.
unresolved: Verify both source forms and inflections, then reconstruct whether i retention or later analogical readdition explains the contour contrast.
